messages.author: 6d3f7222550fe21b
messages.subject: binwidth, histograms of 2 different variables
parts:
Consider a dataset with two very differently distributed variables.

set.seed(3)
DAATA<-data.frame(
ONE = rnorm(50)
, TWO = exp(exp(rnorm(50)))
)

# We want to make two histograms, one over the other, on the same figure
# region, so that the shapes of the two distributions can be readily
# compared. In traditional graphics:

par(mfrow=c(2,1))
hist( DAATA$ONE)
hist(DAATA$TWO)

# In ggplot2:

graphics.off()
require(ggplot2)
Loong<- melt(DAATA)
print(summary(Loong))

print(
ggplot(data=Loong, aes(x= value, y=..density..))
+ geom_histogram()
+ facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)
)

# But how do we control the binwidth in the two different histograms?
# To specify a single binwidth value makes no sense for these two very
# different variables:

print(
ggplot(data=Loong, aes(x= value, y=..density..))
+ geom_histogram(binwidth=1 )
+ facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)
)

# And to specify binwidth as a vector returns an error:

print(
ggplot(data=Loong, aes(x= value, y=..density..))
+ geom_histogram(binwidth=c(1,50) )
+ facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)
)

This is a place where it would be nice to be able to specify the number of bins rather than the binwidth.

Is there a ggplot2 solution to this?

Thanks for any insights

Jacob A. Wegelin
Assistant Professor
Department of Biostatistics

parts:
Hi

perhaps it is simple solution to calculate by yourself before plot like this:

set.seed(3)
d1 <- data.frame(ONE = rnorm(50), TWO = exp(exp(rnorm(50))))
d2 <- melt(d1)

d2$bw <- c(ONE=1, TWO=50)[d2$variable]
d3 <- ddply(d2, .(variable), function(x)data.frame(bin(x$value,
binwidth=x$bw[1])))

ggplot(data=d3, aes(x, density)) +
geom_histogram(stat="identity") +
facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)

--

Dear Dr. Takahashi:

Thank you for this solution. But I see a problem in this. The bars in the histogram do not touch, so that it looks like a barchart instead of a histogram.

The problem can be simplified to the following:

graphics.off(); dev.new(); dev.new()
set.seed(3); a2<-data.frame(value=sort(rnorm(50)))
a3<-data.frame(bin(a2$value, binwidth=1/5))
dev.set(2)
ggplot(a2, aes(x=value))+ geom_histogram(binwidth=1/5)
dev.set(3)
ggplot(a3, aes(x=x, y=density)) + geom_histogram(stat="identity")

Incidentally, this is a place where it would be nice to have a way to place two plots over each other in ggplot2, as one would do with

par(mfrow=c(2,1))

in traditional graphics.

Jacob Wegelin

messages.author: 6d3f7222550fe21b
messages.subject: Re: binwidth, histograms of 2 different variables
parts:
Here is almost a complete solution.

Thanks to Kohske Takahashi and Hadley Wickham, cf. https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Align-two-plots-on-a-page/.

set.seed(3)
DAATA<-data.frame(
ONE = rnorm(50)
, TWO = exp(exp(rnorm(50)))
)

# We want to make two histograms, one over the other, on the same figure
# region, so that the shapes of the two distributions can be readily
# compared. In traditional graphics:

par(mfrow=c(2,1))
hist( DAATA$ONE, main="", xlab="Log of something")
hist(DAATA$TWO, main="", xlab="Count of cells or something" )

# And we also want to control the binwidth for the two very different distributions.
# In ggplot2:

require(ggplot2)
Loong<- melt(DAATA)
Loong$verboseVar<-factor(
c( ONE="Log of something", TWO="Count of cells or something")[Loong$variable]
, levels=c(
"Log of something"
,
"Count of cells or something"
)
)
print(summary(Loong))

dfONE<- Loong[Loong$variable=="ONE",]
dfTWO<- Loong[Loong$variable=="TWO",]

stuff<- ggplot(data=Loong, mapping=aes(x=value) )
stuff<- stuff + facet_wrap( ~ verboseVar , scale="free", nrow=2)
stuff<- stuff + layer(data=dfONE, geom="histogram", stat="bin", stat_params=list(binwidth=1/2) )
stuff<- stuff + layer(data=dfTWO, geom="histogram", stat="bin", stat_params=list(binwidth=50) )
print(
stuff
+ opts(
plot.title=theme_blank()
, axis.title.x=theme_blank()
)
)

# One remaining complaint: The units are not identified under the X axis of each panel, so I put it into the strip at the top of each panel.

Simon, melt() is in the reshape package. With the new version of
ggplot2, you now need to load this explicitly, i.e. "library(reshape)"
before using.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: binwidth, histograms of 2 different variables
parts:
Thanks, so I used library(reshape2), which did define a melt() function.

Still the same error messages. This solution doesn't work :(

I must admit I've haven't got time to look into what layer() does, which is where the error message is generated. Anyone out there with the time?

Simon

On Friday, September 28, 2012 5:43:04 PM UTC+1, Ben wrote:
Simon, melt() is in the reshape package. With the new version of
ggplot2, you now need to load this explicitly, i.e. "library(reshape)"
before using.

Ben

> On Monday, April 18, 2011 6:12:40 PM UTC+1, Jacob Wegelin wrote:
>>
>>
>> Here is almost a complete solution.
>>
>> Thanks to Kohske Takahashi and Hadley Wickham, cf.
>> https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Align-two-plots-on-a-page/.
>>
>> set.seed(3)
>> DAATA<-data.frame(
>>           ONE = rnorm(50)
>>           , TWO = exp(exp(rnorm(50)))
>> )
>>
>> # We want to make two histograms, one over the other, on the same figure
>> # region, so that the shapes of the two distributions can be readily
>> # compared. In traditional graphics:
>>
>> par(mfrow=c(2,1))
>> hist( DAATA$ONE, main="", xlab="Log of something")
>> hist(DAATA$TWO, main="", xlab="Count of cells or something" )
>>
>> # And we also want to control the binwidth for the two very different
>> distributions.
>> # In ggplot2:
>>
>> require(ggplot2)
>> Loong<- melt(DAATA)
>> Loong$verboseVar<-factor(
>>          c( ONE="Log of something", TWO="Count of cells or
>> something")[Loong$variable]
>>          , levels=c(
>>                  "Log of something"
>>                  ,
>>                  "Count of cells or something"
>>                  )
>>          )
>> print(summary(Loong))
>>
>> dfONE<- Loong[Loong$variable=="ONE",]
>> dfTWO<- Loong[Loong$variable=="TWO",]
>>
>> stuff<- ggplot(data=Loong, mapping=aes(x=value) )
>> stuff<- stuff + facet_wrap( ~ verboseVar , scale="free", nrow=2)
>> stuff<- stuff + layer(data=dfONE, geom="histogram", stat="bin",
>> stat_params=list(binwidth=1/2) )
>> stuff<- stuff + layer(data=dfTWO, geom="histogram", stat="bin",
>> stat_params=list(binwidth=50) )
>> print(
>>          stuff
>>          + opts(
>>                  plot.title=theme_blank()
>>                  , axis.title.x=theme_blank()
>>                  )
>>          )
>>
>> # One remaining complaint: The units are not identified under the X axis
>> of each panel, so I put it into the strip at the top of each panel.
>>
>>
>> On Sat, 16 Apr 2011, Jacob Wegelin wrote:
>>
>> >
>> > Consider a dataset with two very differently distributed variables.
>> >
>> > set.seed(3)
>> > DAATA<-data.frame(
>> >         ONE = rnorm(50)
>> >         , TWO = exp(exp(rnorm(50)))
>> > )
>> >
>> > # We want to make two histograms, one over the other, on the same figure
>> > # region, so that the shapes of the two distributions can be readily
>> > # compared. In traditional graphics:
>> >
>> > par(mfrow=c(2,1))
>> > hist( DAATA$ONE)
>> > hist(DAATA$TWO)
>> >
>> > # In ggplot2:
>> >
>> > graphics.off()
>> > require(ggplot2)
>> > Loong<- melt(DAATA)
>> > print(summary(Loong))
>> >
>> > print(
>> >         ggplot(data=Loong, aes(x= value, y=..density..))
>> >         + geom_histogram()
>> >         + facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)
>> > )
>> >
>> > # But how do we control the binwidth in the two different histograms? #
>> > To
>> > specify a single binwidth value makes no sense for these two very #
>> > different
>> > variables:
>> >
>> > print(
>> >         ggplot(data=Loong, aes(x= value, y=..density..))
>> >         + geom_histogram(binwidth=1 )
>> >         + facet_wrap( ~ variable , scales="free", ncol=1)
>> > )

>> > # And to specify binwidth as a vector returns an error:

>> > )
>> >
>> > This is a place where it would be nice to be able to specify the number
>> > of

>> >
>> > Is there a ggplot2 solution to this?
